stops.title: The age of iron
stops.blurb: Iron changed what everyday tools and weapons were made of. Smiths in Anatolia had smelted small amounts of iron since the early second millennium BCE, but only after about 1200 BCE did it come into wide use across the Near East. South of the Sahara, people were smelting iron during the first millennium BCE, perhaps earlier. Kush later worked iron on a large scale at Meroe.
stops.dateNote: Iron use grew slowly: small amounts from about 2000 BCE, wide use only from about 1200 to 800 BCE, at different times in different places.
stops.debate: Scholars disagree on whether iron smelting south of the Sahara was invented there or learned from North Africa or the Near East, and on how early it began.

stops.title: Phoenician traders and the alphabet
stops.blurb: The Phoenicians lived in port cities such as Tyre, Sidon and Byblos, on the coast of today's Lebanon. They sold cedar wood, purple dye and metalwork, and by the late 700s BCE had trading posts around the Mediterranean, including Carthage. Their short alphabet of letters for sounds was taken up by the Greeks, and it became the root of most alphabets used in Europe today.
stops.dateNote: Carthage's founding date of 814 BCE comes from later tradition.

stops.title: Bantu-speaking farmers spread across Africa
stops.blurb: Today more than 500 related Bantu languages are spoken across central, eastern and southern Africa. They spread from a homeland in west-central Africa, near today's Cameroon and Nigeria. Over thousands of years, people who farmed more and more moved south through and around the rainforest, then east and south. Their genes show they also mixed with the people already living in each region.
stops.dateNote: The spread began roughly 5,000 to 4,000 years ago and went on for thousands of years. The year shown is a midpoint.
stops.debate: Researchers disagree about whether the first speakers crossed the rainforest early or waited for savannah corridors to open later.

stops.title: The Persian Empire
stops.blurb: From 550 BCE, Cyrus of Persia and his heirs built an empire from Egypt to the Indus valley. Darius I divided it into provinces run by governors and linked them with roads and relay stations. The first coins had been made shortly before in Lydia, which Cyrus conquered. Cyrus also let the Judeans held in Babylon return home. Alexander conquered the empire by 330 BCE.

stops.title: Teachers of a new kind
stops.blurb: In a few centuries, teachers in several regions asked how a person should live. Confucius in China taught ritual and kindness. The Buddha in the Ganges valley taught a middle path to end suffering. Judean scribes reshaped their sacred writings after exile in Babylon, and Greek thinkers argued about the good life. Their schools still shape the beliefs of billions of people.
stops.dateNote: The Buddha's dates are uncertain: older estimates put his death around 480 BCE, many scholars now say around 400 BCE. Confucius traditionally lived 551 to 479 BCE.
stops.debate: Some scholars see a single 'Axial Age' of new ideas; others find that the same traits appeared in different places centuries apart, so there was no single age.

stops.title: From Athens to Alexandria
stops.blurb: In 508 BCE, Cleisthenes reorganized the citizens of Athens and gave a council of 500 more say, a step toward rule by citizens, though women and enslaved people had none. After Alexander's conquests, Egypt's Greek kings founded a great library at Alexandria. Eratosthenes, who ran the library from about 255 BCE, used shadows and distances to estimate the size of the Earth.
stops.dateNote: The library was founded around 295 BCE. The exact accuracy of Eratosthenes' result depends on the length of his 'stadium', which is unknown.

stops.title: Ashoka carves his edicts
stops.blurb: Ashoka ruled the Maurya empire, which covered most of South Asia. After a bloody war in Kalinga, his own inscription says, he felt deep remorse. He had messages carved on rocks and pillars across his lands, urging kindness to people and animals and respect for all religious groups. He supported Buddhist monks, and Buddhism began to spread, including to Sri Lanka.
stops.dateNote: Ashoka reigned from about 273 or 269 to 232 BCE. The Kalinga war came in the eighth year after he was crowned.
stops.debate: Ashoka's fame as a tolerant ruler rests on a small set of inscriptions, and some scholars question how far they describe real policy.

stops.title: Qin and Han unite China
stops.blurb: In 221 BCE the king of Qin conquered his rivals and became China's first emperor. He made one script, one coinage and one set of measures, and built roads. Over 7,000 clay soldiers guard his tomb. The Han dynasty that followed lasted about four centuries, trained officials in Confucian learning, and saw paper come into wide use.
stops.dateNote: Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving paper around 105 CE, but simpler paper existed earlier.

stops.title: Rome's empire of roads
stops.blurb: From 27 BCE, Rome was ruled by emperors, and its empire circled the Mediterranean. A new digital map counts about 300,000 kilometres of Roman roads around 150 CE, though the exact route of most of them is uncertain. Roman builders also mixed concrete with hot lime, which left small lumps that can help seal cracks. Much of their concrete has lasted two thousand years.

stops.title: Silk Roads and monsoon seas
stops.blurb: From the 100s BCE, chains of merchants carried Chinese silk west across Central Asia, and horses, grapes and other goods east. At sea, sailors used the monsoon winds to cross between Egypt's Red Sea ports and India, trading gold for pepper. Ships linked India with Southeast Asia too. Along these routes travelled Buddhist monks, who carried their faith to Central Asia and China.

stops.title: Kush and Aksum
stops.blurb: Along the Nile in today's Sudan, the kingdom of Kush lasted about a thousand years. Its rulers were buried in pyramids at Meroe, a city of iron-working. To the southeast, Aksum in today's Ethiopia and Eritrea grew rich from Red Sea trade through its port of Adulis. It minted its own coins, and in the 300s CE its king Ezana became a Christian.

stops.title: Teotihuacan and the Maya
stops.blurb: Teotihuacan, in the Valley of Mexico, became the largest city in the ancient Americas, with huge pyramids and blocks of apartment compounds. To the southeast, Maya cities such as Tikal raised carved stone monuments that record their kings. Their Long Count calendar, with dates from 36 BCE, later used a sign for zero, an idea worked out here separately from Asia.
stops.dateNote: Teotihuacan grew from about 100 BCE; its centre burned around 550 CE.
stops.debate: Estimates of Teotihuacan's population at its height range widely, from at least 25,000 to as many as 200,000 people.

stops.title: Gupta India and new mathematics
stops.blurb: The Gupta kings united much of northern India in the 300s CE. Buddhist monasteries flourished and Hindu temples multiplied. In 499 CE, near the Gupta capital, the astronomer Aryabhata finished a book of mathematics and astronomy at the age of 23. It gives pi as 3.1416. Indian mathematicians were developing the place-value numbers, with zero, that most of the world now uses.
stops.dateNote: When zero first appeared in Indian writing is unclear, because the Bakhshali manuscript is hard to date.
stops.debate: Radiocarbon tests suggested parts of the Bakhshali manuscript, which uses a dot for zero, are very old, but specialists dispute what those dates mean.

stops.title: Plagues, rebellions and falls
stops.blurb: From about 165 CE a pandemic, probably smallpox, swept the Roman Empire, and another struck around 250. In China, the Yellow Turban rebels rose in 184 behind a Daoist healer, and the Han dynasty ended in 220. In 476 the last Roman emperor in the west was removed, while the Roman Empire in the east carried on.
stops.dateNote: 476 CE is a traditional end date; the western empire had been shrinking for decades.
stops.debate: Estimates of how many people the Antonine pandemic killed range from 2 to 50 percent; recent studies suggest about 10 to 20 percent.

links.label: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

p: Today more than 500 Bantu languages are spoken by about 310 million people, across most of Africa south of the equator. Languages such as Swahili, Zulu, Shona and Kikongo all belong to this one family. They share so much because their speakers' ancestors came from one small region in west-central Africa, near the border of today's Cameroon and Nigeria.

Starting roughly 5,000 to 4,000 years ago, groups of Bantu speakers began to move. Over the following thousands of years they spread south through the rainforest and along its edges, then east toward the Great Lakes and south toward what is now South Africa. Farming became more and more central to their way of life, and in later centuries many communities also worked iron. They did not move into empty land. Hunter-gatherers and herders already lived in many of these regions, and the newcomers often married into those communities.

The evidence comes from two main sources. Linguists compare words across hundreds of living Bantu languages and build family trees showing which languages split from which. By placing each language on a map, they can estimate where and roughly when the splits happened. One study of this kind found that the spread followed open savannah where it could, and that the rainforest slowed it down.

Geneticists compare the DNA of living people. A study of more than 1,700 people found that genetic diversity falls the farther a group lives from western Africa. This is what you would expect if small groups split off again and again as they moved. The same work found that Bantu speakers mixed with local people along the way, and that a region in today's Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo was a crossroads of later movements. DNA from ancient skeletons, though still scarce in Africa, adds further checks.

The biggest question is the route. One view holds that early Bantu speakers waited until the rainforest thinned around 2,500 years ago, opening savannah corridors, and then moved south through them. A 2022 study using a larger language tree argued instead that speakers entered the rainforest about 4,400 years ago, before those corridors opened. The dates in all these studies are wide estimates, and different methods give different answers.
There is also debate about why the spread happened. Farming, a growing population and later iron tools are all possible drivers, and they probably mattered in different ways in different places.

The Bantu expansion is one of the largest movements of people and languages in human history. It shaped the languages, farming and genes of hundreds of millions of people living today. It also shows that the great changes of these centuries were not limited to empires with written records.

In 550 BCE Cyrus, a ruler from Persia in southwestern Iran, defeated the king of the Medes. Within about a decade he had taken Lydia and its capital, Sardis, in western Anatolia, and in 539 BCE he entered Babylon. His son Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BCE. Darius I, who ruled from 522 to 486 BCE, pushed the frontier into northwestern India. The result was the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from the Nile to the Indus.

Darius divided the empire into provinces, each run by a governor called a satrap. He built a network of roads with relay stations so that officials and messages could travel fast. Around 518 BCE he began a great terrace at Persepolis, where he and his successors Xerxes I and Artaxerxes I built palaces and halls. Persian rule also changed life for subject peoples. When Cyrus took Babylon, he ended the exile of the Judeans whom the Babylonians had carried off decades before, and many returned to Jerusalem.
The empire fought long wars with Greek cities, losing at Marathon in 490 BCE and at Salamis and Plataea in 480 and 479 BCE. In the 330s BCE Alexander of Macedon conquered it province by province.

Much of the written story comes from Greek authors, especially Herodotus, who were often the empire's enemies. He describes the road from Sardis to Susa, saying it had royal stations all along it, 111 stages in all, and took about 90 days to walk. Persian kings left their own inscriptions, and the ruins of Persepolis show their style of rule: stone reliefs of people from many lands bringing gifts.

Coins are another clue. The earliest known coins were made of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, and were found at the temple of Artemis at Ephesus, near Sardis. A group of them was buried in a pot around 650 to 625 BCE. They were probably issued by a Lydian king. King Croesus of Lydia, whom Cyrus defeated, later issued separate gold and silver coins.

Because so much of the evidence is Greek, historians debate how far it gives a fair picture. Greek writers often showed the Persians as luxurious and tyrannical. Modern scholars try to balance this with Persian, Babylonian and Egyptian sources. The numbers in Herodotus, such as army sizes, are often doubted, though his description of the road fits other evidence for a royal relay system.

The Persian Empire showed that one state could hold together many peoples, languages and religions over a vast area. It did so with roads, provinces and local rulers rather than by forcing one culture on everyone. Later rulers of large empires faced the same problem, and many used similar tools.

Between about 600 and 300 BCE, new kinds of teachers appeared in several parts of Asia and the Mediterranean. They asked how a person should live, what makes a good ruler, and how to escape suffering.

In China, Confucius, traditionally said to have lived from 551 to 479 BCE, came from a small state called Lu. He taught that people become good by practising ritual and by cultivating ren, often translated as kindness or humaneness. In the Ganges valley of northern India, the Buddha taught that suffering comes from craving and that it can end by following a middle path between pleasure and harsh self-denial. In the same region, the Jain tradition was taking shape. Judean scribes, after their exile in Babylon, gathered and reworked the writings that became the Hebrew Bible. Greek thinkers debated the nature of the good life, and later schools such as the Stoics taught self-control.

Most of what we know comes from texts written down later by followers. The Analects, the main collection of sayings of Confucius, was put together long after his death, and scholars disagree about how much of it records his words. The earliest Buddhist texts were passed on by memory before being written down, so even the Buddha's dates are uncertain. Older estimates put his death around 480 BCE; many scholars now favour a date around 400 BCE.

In the twentieth century the philosopher Karl Jaspers called roughly 800 to 200 BCE the "Axial Age". He saw it as a turning point, when several civilizations independently arrived at similar new ideas. Researchers still argue about whether this is real.

One study argued that these traditions arose in places that had become richer. When people had more than enough to survive, the study suggested, they began to value self-control and long-term goals over immediate rewards. Another study used a large database of past societies to test the idea. It found that features linked to the Axial Age, such as moral codes and limits on rulers' power, appeared in different places at very different times, some centuries or even millennia earlier. That undercuts the idea of a single age.

Whatever we call this period, the traditions that began in it are still alive. Confucian, Buddhist, Jain, Jewish and Greek ideas shaped the faiths and philosophies of later centuries. Today they influence how billions of people think about right and wrong, family, and the meaning of a good life.

From the second century BCE, trade across Asia grew sharply. In 101 BCE a Han Chinese army reached Ferghana in Central Asia, in part to obtain its prized horses. Chinese silk travelled west, while goods such as grapes, wine and alfalfa came east. No single merchant made the whole journey. Goods passed along a chain of traders, through oasis towns such as Kashgar and Samarkand, and across the Parthian empire in Iran toward the Mediterranean.

At the same time, sailors learned to use the monsoon, the seasonal winds of the Indian Ocean that blow one way in summer and the other in winter. Ships sailed from Egypt's Red Sea ports, such as Berenike, to the southwest coast of India and back again within a year. Roman gold and silver paid for Indian pepper, spices, gems and cloth. From India, other ships crossed the Bay of Bengal to Southeast Asia, where goods were carried overland across the narrow Kra isthmus and on toward the South China Sea.
Ideas travelled too. Buddhist monks and merchants carried their faith along these routes into Central Asia and then to China.

UNESCO's listing of the Silk Roads describes a network of routes running more than 35,000 kilometres, including a corridor of about 5,000 kilometres linking Chang'an with Central Asia. Han records describe embassies and campaigns. For the sea routes, a Greek merchant's guide called the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes Roman coins being exchanged for pepper at the Indian port of Muziris. Tamil poems speak of foreign traders bringing gold for pepper. At Berenike and Myos Hormos on the Red Sea, archaeologists have found writing in Tamil and in Prakrit, a group of Indian languages. Roman goods turn up at Arikamedu and Pattanam in India.
In Southeast Asia, pendants copying Roman coins have been found at Óc Eo in Vietnam and at sites in Thailand. A stone mould shows that some of them were made locally.

Historians argue about how big this trade was. The Roman writer Pliny claimed that 100 million sesterces a year flowed east, but his figure may be a moral complaint about luxury rather than an accurate count. Scholars also debate who ran the trade. Older accounts put Romans at the centre; newer work stresses the role of Indian merchants and rulers.

These routes linked Han China, the Kushan and Parthian lands, India, Southeast Asia and Rome for the first time in a lasting network. Goods, crops, technologies and religions moved along them for centuries. They are the start of a connected world.

Around 100 BCE, a city began to grow in the northeast of the Valley of Mexico. Its builders laid it out on a grand plan along a broad avenue. Between about 100 and 250 CE they raised enormous monuments, including the Pyramid of the Sun, which measures about 225 by 222 metres at its base and rises about 75 metres. Later, between about 250 and 550 CE, most people lived in large walled apartment compounds. By around 400 CE, Teotihuacan covered about 20 square kilometres and was the largest city in the Americas.
Around 550 CE, fire destroyed much of the city centre. People went on living there, but in much smaller numbers.

To the southeast, in the lowlands of today's Guatemala, Belize and southern Mexico, Maya cities such as Tikal grew powerful. Tikal had been settled since about 600 BCE. Its rulers raised carved stone monuments, called stelae, recording their births, reigns and wars.

Archaeologists have mapped Teotihuacan in detail and excavated many of its compounds. Objects in Teotihuacan style turn up at distant sites such as Tikal, Copán and Monte Albán. Maya inscriptions at Tikal describe ties with Teotihuacan.

The Maya and their neighbours used a Long Count calendar, which counts days from a fixed starting point. The earliest known Long Count date, carved on a monument at Chiapa de Corzo in southern Mexico, corresponds to 36 BCE. The system was inherited from earlier peoples of the Gulf Coast region. Early examples, up to about 162 CE, do not show a zero. Later, a sign for zero appeared, first as a placeholder and later as a number in its own right. This was worked out separately from the zero used in India.

Nobody knows how many people lived in Teotihuacan. UNESCO gives at least 25,000. The Metropolitan Museum of Art cites estimates of 125,000 to 200,000 around 400 CE. The difference depends on how many people are thought to have lived in each compound.

It is also unclear who burned the city centre around 550 CE, or why. Scholars also debate how much power Teotihuacan held over Maya cities: whether it ruled them, traded with them, or mainly served as a powerful example.

Teotihuacan and the Maya cities show that the Americas developed large cities, calendars and writing on their own, without contact with Asia, Africa or Europe. Their zero is a reminder that a key idea in mathematics was invented more than once.
